title: ORDER BY & Sorting Control
description: Sort result sets deterministically, control NULL positioning with NULLS FIRST/LAST, and sort across collations.

data.text: Relational tables are unordered mathematical sets. Without an explicit **`ORDER BY`** clause, PostgreSQL does not guarantee any deterministic order of returned rows. Physical table order can change at any time due to `VACUUM`, page reorganization, or parallel worker scanning.
Controlling NULL Placement with NULLS FIRST and NULLS LAST
By default in PostgreSQL, `ASC` puts NULLs last (`NULLS LAST`), while `DESC` puts NULLs first (`NULLS FIRST`). You can override this behavior explicitly using `NULLS FIRST` or `NULLS LAST`.

data.title: Ordering Tasks with NULL Dates at the End
data.content: Ensuring completed tasks are sorted newest first, while uncompleted (NULL) dates appear at the end.
data.code:
-- Show completed tasks newest first, keeping incomplete tasks (NULL) at the bottom
SELECT id, title, completed_at
FROM tasks
ORDER BY completed_at DESC NULLS LAST, id ASC;

data.title: Index Matching for ORDER BY
data.text: If you create an index with `CREATE INDEX idx_tasks ON tasks (completed_at DESC NULLS LAST)`, PostgreSQL can perform a backward index scan to fulfill the query with zero in-memory sort overhead!

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Query results have no guaranteed order without an explicit `ORDER BY` clause.
Use `NULLS FIRST` or `NULLS LAST` to control where null values appear in sorted results.
Always include a unique tie-breaker column (e.g. `id`) for deterministic pagination.
